Yes. The cleanest theoretical way to study this is through **Bayes classification error**, because it gives you a population-level statement about what happens when you add predictors. Then you can contrast that with the finite-sample behavior of an estimated classifier.

Suppose $Y\in{1,\ldots,K}$ and you currently classify using predictors $X$. The Bayes classifier is

$$
g^*(X)=\arg\max_k P(Y=k\mid X),
$$

and its minimum possible misclassification rate is

$$
R^*(X)
=
P\{g^*(X)\neq Y\}
=
1-E\left[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X)\right].
$$

Now add a new predictor $Z$. Then

$$
R^*(X,Z)
=
1-E\left[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X,Z)\right].
$$

A fundamental result is

$$
\boxed{R^*(X,Z)\le R^*(X).}
$$

So, **at the population/Bayes level, adding information can never make the optimal MCR worse**. It either decreases MCR or leaves it unchanged.

There is a very nice proof. Since

$$
P(Y=k\mid X)
=
E[P(Y=k\mid X,Z)\mid X],
$$

and $\max(\cdot)$ is convex,

$$
\max_k E[p_k(X,Z)\mid X]
\le
E[\max_k p_k(X,Z)\mid X].
$$

Taking expectations,

$$
E[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X)]
\le
E[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X,Z)],
$$

and therefore

$$
R^*(X,Z)\le R^*(X).
$$

For binary classification this is particularly transparent. Let

$$
\eta(X)=P(Y=1\mid X).
$$

Then

$$
R^*(X)
=
E[\min\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}]
$$

or equivalently

$$
R^*(X)
=
\frac12-
E\left|\eta(X)-\frac12\right|.
$$

Adding $Z$ can make the posterior probabilities move farther away from $0.5$, allowing more confident—and sometimes different—classifications.

### But here is the crucial distinction

The above result is **not** saying that adding variables to logistic regression, LDA, a tree, etc. must improve test-set MCR.

There are really two different statements:

| Situation                                    | Effect of adding $Z$ |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| True Bayes classifier / infinite information | MCR cannot increase  |
| Classifier estimated from finite data        | MCR can increase     |

The second phenomenon is extremely important. With finite $n$, additional predictors introduce additional estimation variance and model complexity. Eventually the deterioration in estimation can outweigh the additional predictive information.

This is the classical **Hughes phenomenon**, sometimes called the **peaking phenomenon** or related to the curse of dimensionality. Hughes' 1968 paper showed that, for fixed sample size, expected classification accuracy can initially improve as the number of measurements grows and then deteriorate. ([DBLP][1])

Conceptually:

$$
\text{more variables}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\begin{cases}
\text{potentially lower Bayes error}\\
\text{but greater estimation difficulty}
\end{cases}
$$

and therefore the observed test MCR might have a U-shaped relationship with model complexity.

This distinction may fit especially well with the framework you have been developing around model/error and prediction: **additional variables reduce the irreducible classification error only insofar as they contain relevant information about $Y$ beyond what $X$ already tells us; but estimating how to use that information introduces sampling error.**

### When does a new variable actually reduce Bayes MCR?

This question is subtler than simply asking whether $Z$ is associated with $Y$.

If

$$
Y\perp Z\mid X,
$$

then

$$
P(Y\mid X,Z)=P(Y\mid X)
$$

and therefore

$$
R^*(X,Z)=R^*(X).
$$

So conditional information is what matters.

But even

$$
Y\not\perp Z\mid X
$$

does **not necessarily imply a reduction in MCR**.

For example, suppose

$$
P(Y=1\mid X)=0.80,
$$

and observing $Z$ changes this to either $.70$ or $.90$. $Z$ clearly contains information about $Y$, but the optimal prediction remains $Y=1$ in every case.

Therefore MCR doesn't necessarily improve.

Contrast this with

$$
P(Y=1\mid X)=0.55,
$$

while after observing $Z$ we get

$$
P(Y=1\mid X,Z)
=
\begin{cases}
.80\\
.30.
\end{cases}
$$

Now $Z$ changes which side of the decision boundary some observations fall on, and Bayes MCR decreases.

That gives an especially useful distinction:

$$
\boxed{\text{predictive information} \neq \text{necessarily MCR improvement}.}
$$

A predictor can improve probability estimation while producing exactly the same hard classifications.

That observation also connects MCR to **entropy/log-loss**. Conditional entropy obeys

$$
H(Y\mid X,Z)\le H(Y\mid X),
$$

with reduction

$$
H(Y\mid X)-H(Y\mid X,Z)
=
I(Y;Z\mid X)\ge0.
$$

So if $Z$ gives conditional information about $Y$, it improves the theoretical information available for probabilistic prediction. But MCR is much coarser because it only cares about the winning class.

That may be particularly relevant if you are trying to build a theoretical bridge among **MCR, entropy, and PRE**.

## References I would start with

**1. Devroye, Györfi & Lugosi (1996), *A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition*.**
This is probably the strongest theoretical reference for what you're asking. Chapter 2 is literally **“The Bayes Error”**, followed by chapters on inequalities, classification rules, consistency, error estimation, complexity regularization, and feature extraction. ([DOI][2])

I would use this as the main mathematical source for

$$
R(g)=P(g(X)\neq Y),
$$

Bayes risk,

$$
R^*=\inf_g R(g),
$$

posterior-class probabilities, consistency, and theoretical classification error.

**2. Hughes, G. F. (1968), “On the Mean Accuracy of Statistical Pattern Recognizers,” IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 14(1), 55–63.**
This is the classic paper for the counterpoint: adding features does not necessarily improve an *estimated* classifier when the training sample is finite. ([DBLP][1])

This is particularly useful if your argument is:

$$
\text{population: more information cannot hurt}
$$

versus

$$
\text{sample: more dimensions can hurt estimation}.
$$

**3. Cover & Hart (1967), “Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification.”**
A foundational classification-error paper. They connect nearest-neighbor error to the Bayes error and show the famous asymptotic bound for 1-NN. ([OA Monitor Ireland][3])

For binary classification one form of the result is

$$
R^*\le R_{NN}\le 2R^*(1-R^*)\le2R^*.
$$

It is useful for establishing the Bayes error as the fundamental benchmark against which classification methods are judged.

**4. Blackwell (1951, 1953), comparison of statistical experiments.**
This is a more abstract but surprisingly relevant direction. Blackwell's theory formalizes what it means for one information structure to be “more informative” than another: more information cannot increase optimal Bayes risk for a decision problem. ([Celebratio][4])

Your $X$ versus $(X,Z)$ problem is essentially a special case of this idea.

**5. Feature-selection literature.**
Li et al.'s review organizes feature selection into information-theoretic, statistical, similarity-based, and sparse-learning approaches. ([arXiv][5]) It is useful for moving from the theoretical question

> Does $Z$ contain additional information about $Y$?

to the practical question

> How do we decide which $Z$ to include?

The literature on the Hughes/peaking phenomenon emphasizes exactly the finite-sample tradeoff: true discriminatory information can increase with dimensionality while estimated classifier performance eventually deteriorates. ([OUP Academic][6])

---

I think there is a **very interesting theoretical thread for your framework** here:

$$
\text{Variable added}
\rightarrow
\text{conditional information}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced uncertainty}
\rightarrow
\text{possibly changed predictions}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced MCR}.
$$

But the arrows are not all equivalences. In particular,

$$
I(Y;Z\mid X)>0
$$

can reduce entropy without reducing MCR, because the probabilities may change without changing the modal prediction.

This suggests treating **entropy reduction as a finer notion of predictive improvement than MCR reduction**. MCR only notices improvements that matter enough to change the winning category.

Given your earlier interest in connecting **PRE, $\chi^2$, entropy, and categorical modeling**, I think this is probably the direction worth pursuing. I can next build a **theoretical map showing the relationships among MCR, Bayes error, entropy, Gini impurity, conditional mutual information, and PRE**, including the relevant inequalities and proofs.

# More on Proof
Yes. The proof I sketched is essentially a **Jensen's inequality + posterior probability** argument, and most classification books do not present it exactly in that compact form. For learning it carefully, I would split the reading into two pieces: first the Bayes-classification part, then the convexity/Jensen part.

The best classification reference is **Devroye, Györfi, and Lugosi, *A Probabilistic Theory of Pattern Recognition* (1996)**. Their early chapters develop Bayes error, posterior probabilities, and the optimal classifier carefully. Even if they do not phrase the “adding a variable cannot worsen Bayes error” result exactly as I did, they provide the machinery needed to derive it cleanly.

For the convexity step, I would use **Boyd and Vandenberghe, *Convex Optimization***. Their treatment of convex functions includes the key fact that a pointwise maximum of affine—and more generally convex—functions is convex. Their book is freely available from Stanford. ([Stanford University][1])

Here is the specific piece you need.

Let

$$
f(p_1,\ldots,p_K)=\max\{p_1,\ldots,p_K\}.
$$

Why is this convex?

For any two probability vectors $p$ and $q$, and $0\le\lambda\le1$,

$$
f(\lambda p+(1-\lambda)q)
=
\max_k\{\lambda p_k+(1-\lambda)q_k\}.
$$

For every particular $k$,

$$
p_k\le\max_j p_j
$$

and

$$
q_k\le\max_j q_j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\lambda p_k+(1-\lambda)q_k
\le
\lambda\max_jp_j+(1-\lambda)\max_jq_j.
$$

This is true for **every** $k$, so it is also true for the largest left-hand side:

$$
\boxed{
\max_k\{\lambda p_k+(1-\lambda)q_k\}
\le
\lambda\max_kp_k+(1-\lambda)\max_kq_k
}.
$$

But that is exactly the definition of convexity.

So the slightly mysterious statement

$$
\text{"max is convex"}
$$

is actually quite elementary once written this way.

Now we can revisit the classification proof more slowly.

Suppose

$$
p_k(X,Z)=P(Y=k\mid X,Z).
$$

Before seeing $Z$, our posterior probabilities are

$$
P(Y=k\mid X).
$$

By the law of iterated expectation,

$$
P(Y=k\mid X)
=
E[P(Y=k\mid X,Z)\mid X].
$$

So we may write

$$
P(Y=k\mid X)=E[p_k(X,Z)\mid X].
$$

The probability of being correct under the Bayes classifier using only $X$ is

$$
\max_k P(Y=k\mid X).
$$

Substitute the conditional expectation:

$$
\max_k E[p_k(X,Z)\mid X].
$$

Now Jensen's inequality enters. Because $\max$ is convex,

$$
\max_k E[p_k(X,Z)\mid X]
\le
E\left[\max_k p_k(X,Z)\mid X\right].
$$

The left side is the best probability of correct classification **before observing $Z$**.

The right side is the average best probability of correct classification **after observing $Z$**.

That is the entire argument.

Taking expectation over $X$ gives

$$
E\left[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X)\right]
\le
E\left[\max_k P(Y=k\mid X,Z)\right].
$$

Since Bayes MCR is

$$
R^*=1-P(\text{correct classification}),
$$

we reverse the direction:

$$
\boxed{
R^*(X,Z)\le R^*(X).
}
$$

There is also a much more intuitive way of understanding the proof that does not require Jensen at first. Imagine that after observing $X$ you have three class probabilities

$$
(.50,.30,.20).
$$

Your best classification probability is $.50$.

Now suppose $Z$ can take two equally likely values and yields posterior probabilities

$$
Z=0:\quad(.70,.20,.10),
$$

and

$$
Z=1:\quad(.30,.40,.30).
$$

Averaging them gives

$$
\frac12(.70,.20,.10)+
\frac12(.30,.40,.30)
=
(.50,.30,.20),
$$

so ignoring $Z$ takes you back to the original posterior.

Without $Z$, your probability of being correct is

$$
\max(.50,.30,.20)=.50.
$$

With $Z$, your average probability of being correct is

$$
\frac12(.70)+\frac12(.40)=.55.
$$

So

$$
\max(\text{average probabilities})
\le
\text{average of the maximum probabilities}.
$$

That sentence is Jensen's inequality in this problem.

For the binary case, the geometry becomes even simpler. Write

$$
\eta(X)=P(Y=1\mid X).
$$

Then the Bayes probability of correct classification is

$$
\max\{\eta(X),1-\eta(X)\}.
$$

But

$$
\max\{\eta,1-\eta\}
=
\frac12+\left|\eta-\frac12\right|.
$$

Consequently,

$$
R^*(X)
=
\frac12-E\left|\eta(X)-\frac12\right|.
$$

Adding $Z$ gives

$$
R^*(X,Z)
=
\frac12-
E\left|
P(Y=1\mid X,Z)-\frac12
\right|.
$$

Since

$$
\eta(X)
=
E[\eta(X,Z)\mid X],
$$

convexity of absolute value gives

$$
\left|
E[\eta(X,Z)\mid X]-\frac12
\right|
\le
E\left[
\left|\eta(X,Z)-\frac12\right|
\mid X
\right].
$$

This is just Jensen again, now using the familiar convex function

$$
f(t)=|t|.
$$

I actually think **this binary proof is the better one pedagogically**. It makes the substantive meaning very clear:

$$
R^*
=
\frac12-
\underbrace{
E\left|\eta-\frac12\right|
}_{\text{average separation from uncertainty}}.
$$

Additional information $Z$ can only increase, on average, how far posterior probabilities spread away from their conditional mean. That is exactly what convexity captures.

For deeper theoretical context, **Blackwell's comparison-of-experiments theory** is the more general result behind this. It says, roughly, that having a more informative experiment cannot produce higher optimal Bayes risk for a decision problem. A useful statistical treatment is Goel and DeGroot's *Comparison of Experiments and Information Measures*, which explicitly frames informativeness in terms of expected Bayes risk. ([DOI][2]) A recent paper also gives a modern discussion and proof of Blackwell's theorem. ([DOI][3])

So I would recommend this learning sequence:

1. **Devroye, Györfi & Lugosi** — Bayes classifier and Bayes error.
2. **Boyd & Vandenberghe, §3.2–3.3** — convex functions, pointwise maxima, and Jensen's inequality. ([Stanford University][1])
3. Re-derive the **binary $|\eta-.5|$ proof** yourself.
4. Then look at **Blackwell's theorem** to see that this result is part of a much broader theory of “more information cannot hurt an optimal decision maker.” ([DOI][3])

One thing I find especially promising for your framework is that the binary formula

$$
\boxed{
R^*=\frac12-E\left|\eta-\frac12\right|
}
$$

gives you a very concrete bridge between **prediction, variation in conditional probabilities, and reduction in classification error**. It may be a cleaner starting point than entropy if your eventual goal is to develop an intuitive categorical analogue of your numerical-modeling framework.
